title: Importance, problems and prospects of vegetable crops production in Ethiopia
competency: Explain what vegetables are, their importance, and the potentials and constraints of vegetable production in Ethiopia.

en.text: Vegetables are plants whose fruit, seeds, roots, tubers, bulbs, stems, leaves or flowers are eaten as food. Most are herbaceous, and they may be annual, biennial or perennial. Unlike field grain crops, they are harvested fresh with high moisture, so they are seasonal, perishable, bulky for their value and need intensive management.

screens.title: Fresh or dry?
screens.ask: A farmer harvests teff when the grain is dry. When is a tomato usually harvested?
opts: Fresh, while its moisture is high
Only when it is completely dry
After storing it for a year
screens.after: Vegetables are harvested fresh, with high moisture. Grain crops are harvested at the mature, dry stage.

The part may be fruit, seeds, roots, tubers, bulbs, stems, leaves or flowers.
Many are herbaceous: no persistent woody stem above ground.
Some are annuals, others biennials, still others perennials.
Growth habits: viny, shrubby or tree.

Field grain crops are harvested at the mature stage.

en.text: Ethiopia's most important vegetables include pepper, Ethiopian mustard/kale, onion, tomato, potato, chili, carrot, garlic and cabbage. Over 6.7 million households lived from vegetables in 2018, and exports to the Middle East, Europe, Djibouti and Somalia earn hundreds of millions of dollars. Vegetables give higher value and income than cereals, create jobs, supply processors, and fight hidden hunger with vitamins and minerals; legumes add protein.

screens.title: How many households?
screens.ask: About how many Ethiopian households made their living from vegetables in 2018?
screens.after: The book estimates over 6.7 million households (2018). Vegetables are a big part of the economy.

screens.title: Main vegetables in Ethiopia
paras: Most important: pepper, Ethiopian mustard/kale, onion, tomato, potato, chili, carrot, garlic, cabbage.
Also important: green beans, asparagus, broccoli, celery, cucumbers.
Mainly for home use: cabbages, tomatoes and garlic.
Mainly for export: green beans and peas.
Smallholders (about 0.9 ha) grow mainly for their own use.
Commercial private farms grow only for the market.

screens.title: Economic importance
paras: Over 6.7 million households lived from vegetables (2018 estimate).
Exports earn hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
Buyers: the Middle East, Europe, Djibouti and Somalia.
Tomato and chilli are among the major exports.
Vegetables have a shorter growth cycle and higher value than cereals.
They create jobs and raise household income.
They supply local industries making tomato paste and juices.

screens.title: Nutrition and health
paras: More vegetables reduce hidden hunger: lack of vitamins and minerals.
They are rich in vitamin A, vitamin C, thiamine, niacin, folic acid and beta carotene.
The body turns beta carotene into vitamin A.
Vitamin A is needed for normal vision; long deficiency leads to blindness.
Leafy vegetables such as spinach supply iron and other minerals.
Leguminous vegetables (beans, peas) are rich in protein.
screens.note: Corrected wording: the book says beta carotene itself works in vision and that leafy vegetables are rich in protein. See teacher notes.

en.text: Ethiopia has a favourable and diverse climate (altitude from 126 m below to 4620 m above sea level, humid tropics to alpine), abundant labour, and vast land and water. Production is growing thanks to health awareness, small-scale irrigation, investor support, tax incentives, local demand and exports. Yet production is held back by poor knowledge, low consumption, costly inputs, poor management, few processors, poor soils, pests, drought, postharvest losses and costly pump fuel.

opts: Different altitudes give climates for many crops

notes.text: p.4: the book says beta carotene itself works in the visual process and its deficiency leads to blindness. Strictly, the body converts beta carotene to vitamin A; vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and then blindness. The lesson teaches this chain.

p.3: vegetables are not a meaningful iodine source (iodised salt is), and tomato is a weak iron/zinc source; leafy vegetables like spinach supply iron. p.4: legumes, not leafy vegetables, are the protein-rich vegetables. The book lines are not used in graded items.

Typos and garbles: p.2 "plants that that"; "bulky in relation to their volume" should be "value"; p.3 "They smallholders"; p.5 income sentence garbled (meaning: income per hectare from vegetables is higher than from teff or maize).
p.4: altitudes are usually quoted as about 125 m below sea level (Dallol) and 4,550–4,620 m (Ras Dashen). The book's 126 m and 4620 m are kept.
Added: the constraint table grouping, the constraint–solution match and the altitude-range challenge.
